topographicSurvey.title: What is a topographic survey?
topographicSurvey.seoDescription: Learn what a topographic survey is, what information it provides and when it is required for construction, engineering and land management projects in the Canary Islands.
topographicSurvey.intro: A topographic survey is the process of accurately measuring and mapping the natural and man-made features of a piece of land. It provides essential information about elevations, boundaries, structures, vegetation, roads, utilities and terrain characteristics. Topographic surveys are widely used in engineering, construction, architecture, land development and infrastructure projects.
topographicSurvey.section1: What information does a topographic survey provide?
topographicSurvey.section1Text: A topographic survey collects precise data about the shape and characteristics of the terrain. The resulting plans typically show contour lines, spot levels, buildings, walls, roads, fences, trees, drainage systems and other visible features. This information helps engineers, architects and developers make informed decisions during project planning and design.
topographicSurvey.section2: When is a topographic survey required?
topographicSurvey.section2Text: Topographic surveys are commonly required before construction projects, property developments, road works, utility installations, environmental studies and land subdivision processes. They provide the accurate ground information necessary for safe and efficient project execution.
topographicSurvey.section3: How is a topographic survey carried out?
topographicSurvey.section3Text: Surveyors use advanced instruments such as GNSS receivers, robotic total stations and drones to collect field measurements. The data is then processed using specialized software to generate detailed maps, digital terrain models and engineering drawings.
topographicSurvey.section4Text: Modern surveying relies on high-precision technology including GPS/GNSS systems, total stations, laser scanners and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). These tools allow surveyors to achieve high accuracy while reducing fieldwork time.
topographicSurvey.section5Text: Accurate topographic information reduces project risks, improves design quality, minimizes costly construction errors and supports better decision-making throughout the project lifecycle.
topographicSurvey.section6: Topographic surveys in the Canary Islands
topographicSurvey.section6Text: The varied terrain of the Canary Islands makes topographic surveys particularly important. Accurate terrain information is essential for construction projects, infrastructure development, environmental management and property boundary verification across the archipelago.
topographicSurvey.section7Text: The cost and duration of a survey depend on the size, accessibility and complexity of the site. Small residential surveys may take a few hours, while large infrastructure projects may require several days of fieldwork and data processing.
topographicSurvey.section8Text: TOPOATLANTICO provides professional surveying services throughout the Canary Islands. Contact us to discuss your project and request a quotation.

settingOut.title: What is construction setting out?
settingOut.seoDescription: Learn what construction setting out is, when it is required and how it ensures the accurate positioning of structures, installations and earthworks in the Canary Islands.
settingOut.intro: Construction setting out is the process of transferring the dimensions and coordinates from engineering drawings onto the ground before and during construction. It ensures that every element of a project is built in the correct position, elevation and alignment. Accurate setting out is essential for buildings, roads, bridges, utilities and civil engineering projects throughout the Canary Islands.
settingOut.section1Text: Setting out consists of marking the exact location of foundations, columns, walls, roads, drainage systems and all structural elements according to the approved design. Surveyors use precise coordinates to ensure the construction matches the engineering plans.
settingOut.section2Text: Setting out is required before excavation begins and throughout the entire construction process. It is commonly performed for residential developments, commercial buildings, industrial facilities, roads, retaining walls, utilities, bridges and renewable energy projects.
settingOut.section3Text: Professional surveyors use robotic total stations, GNSS receivers and digital levels to transfer design coordinates onto the site with millimetre accuracy. Measurements are continuously checked to guarantee compliance with project specifications.
settingOut.section4Text: Even small positioning errors can lead to costly delays, structural problems and expensive corrections. Accurate setting out reduces construction risks, improves quality control and minimizes rework.
settingOut.section5: Setting out for civil engineering projects
settingOut.section5Text: Large infrastructure projects require continuous survey control throughout construction. Roads, pipelines, railways and earthworks depend on precise setting out to achieve the required geometry and design tolerances.
settingOut.section6: Construction setting out in the Canary Islands
settingOut.section6Text: The complex terrain and volcanic geology of the Canary Islands make precise surveying particularly important. Professional setting out ensures that construction projects adapt correctly to existing terrain conditions while complying with engineering requirements.
settingOut.section7Text: The duration of setting out depends on the size and complexity of the project. Small residential buildings may only require a few hours, whereas large civil engineering projects require continuous survey support throughout construction.

FotogrametriaDrones.title: Drone photogrammetry in the Canary Islands
FotogrametriaDrones.seoDescription: Learn how drone photogrammetry is used to create orthophotos, point clouds and 3D terrain models for surveying, engineering and construction projects in the Canary Islands.
FotogrametriaDrones.intro: Drone photogrammetry has revolutionised the way topographic and cartographic surveys are carried out. By combining unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), high-resolution cameras and specialised processing software, it is now possible to obtain highly accurate geospatial information in a fraction of the time required by traditional surveying methods. At TOPOATLANTICO, we use this technology to produce orthophotos, digital terrain models, dense point clouds and 3D models for engineering, construction, urban planning and environmental projects throughout the Canary Islands.
FotogrametriaDrones.section1Text1: Drone photogrammetry is a surveying technique that reconstructs the geometry of land, buildings or infrastructure by processing aerial photographs captured by an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). Unlike a conventional photograph, each image contains spatial information which, when combined with hundreds or even thousands of overlapping photographs, allows highly accurate three-dimensional models to be generated.
FotogrametriaDrones.section1Text2: The technique is based on digital photogrammetry. Specialised software automatically identifies thousands of common points between consecutive photographs and calculates their position in three-dimensional space. The result is a highly detailed digital representation of the surveyed area with centimetre-level accuracy, particularly when supported by Ground Control Points (GCPs) or GNSS RTK/PPK positioning systems.
FotogrametriaDrones.section1Text3: Today, drone photogrammetry has become an essential tool for surveyors, engineers, architects and public authorities. Its ability to document large areas quickly and safely makes it the preferred solution for civil engineering projects, mining operations, precision agriculture, infrastructure inspections, environmental studies and land management.
FotogrametriaDrones.section2: How is a drone photogrammetric survey carried out?
FotogrametriaDrones.section2Text1: Every project begins with careful flight planning. At this stage, parameters such as flight altitude, Ground Sample Distance (GSD), image overlap, flight speed and the survey area are defined. Proper planning is essential to achieve the required level of accuracy while avoiding unnecessary repeat flights.
FotogrametriaDrones.section2Text2: During the mission, the drone follows a pre-programmed autonomous flight path while capturing a large number of high-resolution georeferenced photographs. Depending on the size and complexity of the project, the survey may consist of anything from a few dozen images to several thousand photographs.
FotogrametriaDrones.section2Text3: Once the flight has been completed, all images are processed using specialised photogrammetry software such as WebODM, Pix4D or Agisoft Metashape. During processing, the photographs are aligned to generate a dense point cloud, from which orthophotos, Digital Terrain Models (DTMs), Digital Surface Models (DSMs) and three-dimensional models are produced for direct use in CAD and GIS software.
FotogrametriaDrones.section3Text1: One of the greatest advantages of drone photogrammetry is the wide variety of deliverables that can be generated from a single flight. The collected data can be processed into different products depending on the requirements of each project, ranging from simple orthophotos to highly detailed three-dimensional engineering models.
FotogrametriaDrones.section3Text2: The most common deliverables include high-resolution georeferenced orthophotos, Digital Terrain Models (DTMs), Digital Surface Models (DSMs), dense point clouds in LAS/LAZ format, textured 3D meshes (OBJ), contour lines and accurate volume calculations for earthworks, stockpiles and quarry operations.
FotogrametriaDrones.section3Text3: These deliverables can be seamlessly integrated into industry-standard software such as AutoCAD Civil 3D, QGIS, ArcGIS and other GIS or CAD platforms, providing engineers, architects and surveyors with reliable geospatial data for design, planning and construction.
FotogrametriaDrones.section4: What level of accuracy can be achieved?
FotogrametriaDrones.section4Text1: One of the most common questions is whether drone photogrammetry can replace a conventional topographic survey. The answer depends on the level of accuracy required. For most mapping, engineering and construction projects, drone photogrammetry is capable of delivering centimetre-level accuracy, provided that the survey is properly planned and carried out using appropriate equipment and methodologies.
FotogrametriaDrones.section4Text2: The final accuracy depends on several factors, including Ground Sample Distance (GSD), camera quality, flight altitude, image overlap, weather conditions and the positioning technology used by the drone. For projects requiring the highest level of accuracy, Ground Control Points (GCPs) measured using GNSS receivers or total stations are commonly incorporated to accurately georeference and optimise the photogrammetric model.
FotogrametriaDrones.section4Text3: Modern drones equipped with RTK or PPK technology significantly reduce the number of Ground Control Points required while improving the absolute positioning of the survey. Nevertheless, for high-precision engineering projects, combining drone photogrammetry with GNSS surveying and strategically placed control points remains the preferred methodology for achieving reliable and verifiable results.
FotogrametriaDrones.section5Text1: One of the greatest advantages of drone photogrammetry is its ability to survey large areas in a remarkably short period of time. Sites that would traditionally require several days of fieldwork can often be documented within a single flight, reducing both project duration and operational costs.
FotogrametriaDrones.section5Text2: In addition to speed, drone surveys provide an exceptional amount of information. A single flight can generate high-resolution orthophotos, Digital Terrain Models (DTMs), Digital Surface Models (DSMs), dense point clouds, three-dimensional meshes and accurate volume calculations. This allows the same dataset to be reused throughout the lifecycle of a project without the need for additional field surveys.
FotogrametriaDrones.section5Text3: Safety is another major benefit. Many surveying projects involve hazardous or difficult-to-access environments such as steep slopes, quarries, industrial roofs, volcanic terrain or unstable ground. Drone technology enables these areas to be documented without exposing surveyors to unnecessary risks while maintaining a high level of accuracy.
FotogrametriaDrones.section6: Applications of drone photogrammetry in the Canary Islands
FotogrametriaDrones.section6Text1: The unique volcanic landscape of the Canary Islands makes drone photogrammetry particularly valuable. Ravines, cliffs, lava fields, coastal areas and other challenging environments can be surveyed efficiently, producing highly detailed topographic information that would otherwise be difficult or time-consuming to obtain using conventional methods.
FotogrametriaDrones.section6Text2: At TOPOATLANTICO, we apply drone photogrammetry to civil engineering, urban planning, earthworks monitoring, stockpile volume calculations, construction progress monitoring, infrastructure inspections, renewable energy projects, environmental studies and heritage documentation. The resulting deliverables integrate seamlessly into CAD, BIM and GIS workflows.
FotogrametriaDrones.section6Text3: By combining drone technology with GNSS surveying, robotic total stations and specialised processing software, we deliver accurate and reliable geospatial information tailored to the specific requirements of each project throughout the Canary Islands.
FotogrametriaDrones.section7Text1: Is authorisation required to carry out a drone survey? In Spain, all drone operations must comply with the regulations established by AESA and EASA. Depending on the location of the project, additional restrictions may apply due to controlled airspace, airports, urban environments or protected natural areas. Every professional operation should therefore include a detailed aeronautical assessment before the flight takes place.
FotogrametriaDrones.section7Text2: How large an area can be surveyed in a single flight? This depends on the drone platform, battery endurance, required image resolution and terrain characteristics. Larger projects are normally divided into several autonomous flight missions to ensure adequate image overlap and maintain the required survey accuracy.
FotogrametriaDrones.section7Text3: Looking for a professional drone photogrammetry survey in the Canary Islands? At TOPOATLANTICO, we combine modern surveying technology with extensive experience in geomatics, engineering surveying and cartography to provide accurate, reliable and cost-effective solutions for projects of every scale.

FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.title: Drone Photogrammetry: How to Plan a Flight
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.seoDescription: Learn how to plan a drone photogrammetry flight, choose the flight altitude, configure image overlap and capture suitable images for orthophotos and 3D models.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.intro: Flight planning is one of the most important stages when aiming to achieve the desired results from drone photogrammetry. Before carrying out the flight, it is necessary to analyse the characteristics of the drone, the dimensions of the survey area, the required resolution and any possible environmental or operational constraints. Proper planning makes it possible to obtain images with the resolution and geometry required to generate accurate and high-quality orthophotos, point clouds and 3D models.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section1: Relationship Between the Camera, Flight Altitude and Ground Footprint
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section1Text1: The area of ground recorded in each photograph depends mainly on the characteristics of the camera and the altitude at which the flight is carried out.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section1Text2: With the same camera, increasing the flight altitude also increases the area of ground covered by each photograph. This makes it possible to cover a larger area with fewer images, but at the same time reduces the level of detail recorded on the ground. Conversely, lowering the flight altitude results in a smaller ground footprint, with each photograph representing a smaller area. This allows a higher level of detail to be obtained, although a greater number of photographs will be required to cover the entire survey area
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section1Text3: The relationship between flight altitude and ground footprint should be selected according to the objective of the survey. There is no universally appropriate flight altitude: planning must be adapted to the required resolution, the characteristics of the camera and the type of final product to be generated.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section2: Resolution and GSD: How Much Ground Does Each Pixel Represent?
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section2Text1: One of the main parameters of a photogrammetric flight is GSD, or Ground Sampling Distance. GSD represents the size of each image pixel on the ground and is normally expressed in centimetres per pixel.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section2Text2: Flight altitude has a direct relationship with GSD. As flight altitude increases, each pixel represents a larger portion of the ground, resulting in lower spatial resolution. Conversely, reducing the flight altitude makes it possible to record smaller features.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section2Text3: For example, a flight planned to achieve approximately 2 cm/pixel will provide considerably more detail than one carried out with a GSD of 5 cm/pixel. The required resolution will depend on the purpose of the survey and the level of accuracy that needs to be achieved.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section3: Forward and Side Overlap Between Photographs
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section3Text1: To reconstruct a 3D model using photogrammetry, it is not enough to obtain individual photographs of the survey area. The images must have sufficient overlap so that the software can identify common points between consecutive photographs.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section3Text2: Forward overlap refers to the overlap between consecutive photographs along the flight direction, while side overlap refers to the overlap between adjacent parallel flight lines.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section3Text3: Insufficient overlap can make photogrammetric reconstruction more difficult and may result in areas with insufficient information, errors in the point cloud or problems when generating the orthophoto. For this reason, the overlap percentage should be defined during flight planning according to the type of terrain, the camera and the final product to be generated. In many cases, a forward overlap of 80% and a side overlap of 70% provides a suitable starting point.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section4: Relationship Between Altitude, Speed and Capture Interval
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section4Text1: Flight altitude determines the size of the ground footprint of each photograph, while drone speed and the interval between photographs determine how far the drone travels between consecutive images.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section4Text2: If the drone flies at a given speed and the camera takes a photograph at a specific time interval, we can approximately calculate the distance travelled between two consecutive photographs. This distance must be compatible with the image footprint in order to achieve the desired forward overlap.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section4Text3: For example, if the drone travels at 5 metres per second and the camera takes a photograph every 2 seconds, the drone will travel approximately 10 metres between photographs. If we increase the speed while maintaining the same capture interval, the distance between photographs will increase and the overlap will decrease.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section4Text4: The opposite approach can also be taken: if we want to maintain a given speed but need to increase the overlap, we can reduce the interval between photographs, provided that the camera and flight system are capable of capturing images at the required frequency.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section4Text5: Flight planning therefore involves finding an appropriate combination of altitude, speed, capture interval and camera characteristics. These parameters are directly related, and changing them independently can significantly affect the outcome of the flight.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section4Text6: In addition, speed must be compatible with the exposure settings and lighting conditions. Excessive speed can increase the risk of motion blur, particularly when relatively long exposure times are used.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section5Text1: Drone battery life is another factor that must be considered during flight planning. The area that can be covered in a single flight depends on the available battery life, flight speed, altitude, number of photographs and the characteristics of the mission.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section5Text2: The battery life stated by the manufacturer should be considered as a reference rather than the actual flight time available for photogrammetric work. Wind, temperature, payload, positioning and safety margins can all reduce the effective flight time.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section5Text3: When the survey area is extensive, it may be necessary to divide the survey into several missions or use multiple batteries. Proper planning makes it possible to organise flights while maintaining sufficient battery reserves to return safely to the take-off point and carry out any necessary battery changes.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section6Text1: There are currently several free tools that allow flight missions to be planned digitally before going to the field. These applications allow you to define the work area, set waypoints, configure flight parameters and, in some cases, automatically generate flight routes to cover an area using parallel passes.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section6Text2: <litchi>Litchi Hub</litchi> is a web-based platform that allows you to design flight missions from your browser using waypoints and configure different mission parameters. It is particularly useful for planning a mission in advance and reviewing its route before carrying out the flight. It also allows routes to be transferred to compatible devices for use with a wide range of commercial drones.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section6Text3: <waypointmap>WaypointMap</waypointmap> is another tool designed for planning mapping missions with compatible drones. It allows you to define a work area and generate automated flight routes to cover it. Compatible drones include the DJI Mini 5 Pro, as well as other DJI models.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section6Text4: These tools make flight planning considerably easier, but they do not replace the need for a preliminary assessment of the terrain or the responsibility of the pilot. Before carrying out a mission, it is necessary to check the actual conditions of the area, obstacles, airspace restrictions, weather conditions and all applicable safety requirements.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section7: From Flight Planning to the Photogrammetric Survey
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section7Text1: A properly planned photogrammetric mission makes it possible to obtain a set of photographs with suitable geometry for subsequent processing. These images can be used to generate products such as orthophotos, point clouds, Digital Terrain Models, Digital Surface Models and 3D models.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section7Text2: The quality of the final result depends on the entire workflow and not only on the software used to process the photographs. The camera, flight altitude, GSD, overlap, speed, capture interval, battery life and terrain conditions must all be considered together.
FotogrametriaDronesPlanificarVuelo.section7Text3: Good planning reduces the likelihood of having to repeat the flight and makes it possible to obtain more consistent information that is better suited to the objectives of the survey.

InmatriculacionFincaRegistro.title: Registering a property for the first time in Spain: Georeferenced representation and Cadastre
InmatriculacionFincaRegistro.seoDescription: Need to register a property in Spain for the first time? Learn about the procedure, georeferenced property plans, and the importance of ensuring consistency between the Spanish Cadastre and Land Registry.
InmatriculacionFincaRegistro.intro: In Spain, inmatriculation is the procedure by which a property that has not previously been registered in the Land Registry is registered for the first time. In this process, correctly identifying the physical property is essential. Spanish Land Registry legislation requires properties being registered for the first time to be accompanied by a georeferenced graphical representation that accurately identifies their location and boundaries. There must also be consistency between the property's legal description, its graphical representation and the information recorded in the Cadastre.
InmatriculacionFincaRegistro.section1: Georeferenced graphical representation and why it matters
InmatriculacionFincaRegistro.section1Text: A georeferenced graphical representation allows the description of a property to be located precisely on the ground using geographic coordinates. In first-registration procedures, Spanish Mortgage Law requires the property's georeferenced graphical representation to be incorporated into the Land Registry, allowing its location, area and boundaries to be accurately identified. In the case of first registration under Article 205, a descriptive and graphical cadastral certificate must be provided together with the deed, and the description of the property in the registration deed must correspond to the cadastral information. This verification is particularly important to prevent the property being registered from overlapping with other registered properties, neighbouring parcels or public land.
InmatriculacionFincaRegistro.section2: How is the property's correspondence with the cadastre checked?
InmatriculacionFincaRegistro.section2Text: Before starting the registration procedure, it is advisable to check that the property's description, area, boundaries and graphical representation are consistent with the cadastral mapping. When differences exist between the physical reality, the documentary description and the Cadastre, it may be necessary to analyse the origin of those discrepancies and determine the appropriate way to resolve them. This may involve topographic surveys, GNSS and total station measurements, cadastral mapping, orthophotography and other cartographic sources. The objective is to accurately determine the property's boundaries and verify that the proposed graphical representation corresponds to the actual portion of land that is intended to be registered.
InmatriculacionFincaRegistro.section3: Documentation and checks before registering a property
InmatriculacionFincaRegistro.section3Text: The documentation required will depend on the procedure used and the specific circumstances of the property. For first registration under Article 205 of the Spanish Mortgage Law, among other requirements, the relevant public deed and the descriptive and graphical cadastral certificate must be provided, with the necessary correspondence between them. Before submitting the documentation to the Land Registry, it is advisable to check the cadastral situation, the possible existence of neighbouring registered properties, the physical boundaries of the land and any potential overlap with roads, public rights of way or other public land. A professional topographic survey and a correctly prepared georeferenced graphical representation can help with these checks and identify potential discrepancies before the registration procedure begins. TOPOATLANTICO provides professional topographic surveying and georeferenced graphical documentation services for these types of procedures throughout the Canary Islands.

CertificadoGeorreferenciacionCanarias.title: What is a georeferencing certificate and when is it required?
CertificadoGeorreferenciacionCanarias.seoDescription: What is a georeferencing certificate and when is it required? Learn what it contains and how it relates to the Spanish Cadastre and Land Registry in the Canary Islands.
CertificadoGeorreferenciacionCanarias.intro: A georeferencing certificate is a technical document that identifies the location, area and boundaries of a property using precise geographic coordinates. Its purpose is to define the parcel graphically and facilitate its identification and correspondence with cadastral and Land Registry information. Depending on the procedure, it may include plans, coordinates of the parcel vertices and supporting graphical documentation required to establish its boundaries.
CertificadoGeorreferenciacionCanarias.section1: When is a georeferencing certificate required?
CertificadoGeorreferenciacionCanarias.section1Text: Georeferencing may be required for various procedures related to property ownership and the Cadastre. These include certain first registrations of properties in the Land Registry, subdivisions, amalgamations and divisions of parcels, modifications to property areas or boundaries, boundary surveys and other procedures where the precise location and geometry of a parcel need to be established. It may also be required to verify the correspondence between the physical reality of a property and its cadastral or Land Registry information.
CertificadoGeorreferenciacionCanarias.section2Text: The content depends on the procedure for which the certificate is required, but a georeferencing certificate may include the identification of the property, area, reference coordinate system, coordinates of the parcel vertices, a georeferenced plan and supplementary graphical documentation. When it is necessary to justify a modification in relation to cadastral mapping, it may also include an alternative graphical representation and the documentation required for its validation.
CertificadoGeorreferenciacionCanarias.section3: How is a georeferencing certificate obtained?
CertificadoGeorreferenciacionCanarias.section3Text: Preparing a georeferencing certificate requires an analysis of the available documentation and a determination of the actual geometry of the property. When the existing information is insufficient, a topographic survey may be carried out using GNSS equipment and a total station. The resulting data is then processed to produce the georeferenced graphical representation, the coordinates of the parcel vertices and the technical documentation required for the relevant procedure. In the Canary Islands, the complex terrain and characteristics of some properties make it particularly important to have precise and correctly georeferenced boundaries.

GmlCatastro.title: What is a cadastral GML file and what is it used for?
GmlCatastro.seoDescription: Learn what a cadastral GML file is, when it is required and how it is generated to provide a georeferenced graphical representation of a property.
GmlCatastro.intro: A GML file is a digital format used to represent the geometry of a parcel or property in a georeferenced form. In Spain, GML files are particularly important in certain procedures involving the Spanish Cadastre and Land Registry, as they allow the location, shape and area of a property to be defined using geographic coordinates.
GmlCatastro.section1: When is a GML file required?
GmlCatastro.section1Text: Whether a GML file is required depends on the procedure being carried out and the characteristics of the property. It may be required for certain first registrations of properties in the Land Registry, subdivisions, amalgamations or divisions of parcels, modifications to property areas or boundaries, and other procedures where a georeferenced graphical representation is required. It can also be used to check the correspondence between the geometry of a property and the cadastral mapping.
GmlCatastro.section2: How is a GML file generated?
GmlCatastro.section2Text: To generate a GML file correctly, it is necessary to have the property's geometry defined by coordinates and using the appropriate reference system. When the available information is not sufficient to determine the property boundaries accurately, a topographic survey using GNSS equipment and a total station may be required. The geometry is then processed and the GML file is generated according to the applicable technical specifications. Before using it in a legal or cadastral procedure, it is advisable to check that the geometry and file data are correct.
GmlCatastro.section3: GML, the Cadastre and the Land Registry
GmlCatastro.section3Text: A GML file provides a digital representation of the georeferenced geometry of a property, but it does not by itself replace the legal or technical documentation required for each procedure. In certain cases, the georeferenced graphical representation must be compared with the cadastral mapping, and differences may need to be explained or supported with technical documentation. Therefore, when discrepancies exist between the physical reality of a property, the Cadastre and the Land Registry, it is advisable to analyse the property's situation before generating or submitting the documentation.

DiferenciaCatastroRegistro.title: What Is the Difference Between the Cadastre and the Land Registry?
DiferenciaCatastroRegistro.seoDescription: Learn the differences between the Spanish Cadastre and Land Registry, what information each contains and why discrepancies may exist between them.
DiferenciaCatastroRegistro.intro: The Spanish Cadastre and the Land Registry are two different institutions that contain information related to real estate. Although their data may be related and should be consistent in certain procedures, their functions and the information they manage are not the same. Understanding these differences is important when buying, selling or regularising a property.
DiferenciaCatastroRegistro.section1: What Is the Cadastre and What Information Does It Contain?
DiferenciaCatastroRegistro.section1Text: The Cadastre is an administrative register containing information about properties, such as their location, area, cadastral reference number, use and graphical representation. Its mapping allows parcels to be identified graphically and their physical and economic characteristics to be consulted. Cadastral information is used, among other purposes, for the management of certain taxes and administrative procedures.
DiferenciaCatastroRegistro.section2Text: The Land Registry is a public register that provides information about the legal status of properties. It records, among other things, ownership rights, mortgages, easements and other charges or rights affecting a property. Registry information is mainly based on the legal documentation submitted for registration.
DiferenciaCatastroRegistro.section3: Why Can Differences Exist Between the Cadastre and Land Registry?
DiferenciaCatastroRegistro.section3Text: Differences may be caused by physical changes to a property that have not been reflected in both institutions, historical errors, differences in area or boundaries, or information originating from documents and maps produced at different times. When discrepancies are detected, it is advisable to analyse the property situation and check the correspondence between the physical reality, the Cadastre and the Land Registry before starting a regularisation procedure.

monitoring.title: Structural monitoring
monitoring.seoDescription: Learn what structural monitoring is, when it is required and how deformation and displacement are monitored in buildings, slopes, tunnels and other structures in the Canary Islands.
monitoring.intro: Structural monitoring is the process of periodically measuring buildings, bridges, retaining walls, dams, excavations and civil engineering structures to detect movements, settlements or deformations before they become critical. Using high-precision surveying techniques, engineers can verify structural stability, improve safety and make informed decisions throughout the entire life cycle of a project.
monitoring.section1Text: Structural monitoring consists of repeatedly measuring specific points on a structure over time. By comparing observations from different surveys, engineers can detect horizontal movements, vertical settlements and structural deformations with millimetre-level accuracy. This information is essential for assessing the real behaviour of the structure and verifying that it performs within the design tolerances.
monitoring.section2Text: Survey monitoring is widely used on buildings, bridges, dams, tunnels, retaining walls, deep excavations, railways, wind farms, slopes and major infrastructure projects. It is also common to monitor nearby buildings during excavation or construction works to ensure that neighbouring properties remain unaffected.
monitoring.section3: How is structural monitoring carried out?
monitoring.section3Text: The process begins by establishing stable control points outside the area affected by the project. Survey prisms or monitoring targets are then installed on the structure and periodically observed using robotic total stations, GNSS receivers or digital levels. The measurements are compared over time to identify any movement or deformation.
monitoring.section4Text: Modern structural monitoring relies on robotic total stations, high-precision GNSS receivers, digital levels, laser scanners and automated monitoring systems. Depending on the project, tilt sensors, crack gauges and other specialized instruments may also be installed to provide continuous structural monitoring.
monitoring.section5Text: Structural monitoring allows engineers to detect movements at an early stage, improve public safety, reduce maintenance costs, prevent major structural failures and provide objective data for engineering decisions. It is an essential quality-control tool throughout the construction and operational phases of infrastructure projects.
monitoring.section6: Benefits of structural monitoring in the Canary Islands
monitoring.section6Text: Structural monitoring allows engineers to detect movements at an early stage, improve public safety, reduce maintenance costs, prevent major structural failures and provide objective data for engineering decisions. The Canary Islands present unique geological conditions due to their volcanic origin, steep terrain and complex landscapes. These characteristics make structural monitoring especially valuable for infrastructure, excavations, retaining structures and major engineering projects, ensuring that any movement is detected before it affects safety or performance.
monitoring.section7Text: The monitoring frequency depends on the structure and its associated level of risk. Some projects require daily observations or fully automated continuous monitoring systems, while others only need monthly or quarterly surveys. Modern surveying equipment is capable of detecting movements of just a few millimetres.
